en: Once the wrapper is cut the surface is exposed and the salt content is far too low to hold bacteria off. Wrap the cut face, keep it at 4 °C or below, and slice off any surface that has gone slimy or smells sour rather than trimming and eating around it.

Not recommended. Freezing wrecks the gel — kamaboko thaws watery and spongy. Japanese producers generally advise against it, and the frozen-product standard of −15 °C or below applies to products made to be frozen, not to a chilled board of kamaboko.

Only the hard, sun-dried balls belong in a cupboard. Keep them bone dry in a sealed jar; if they soften or bloom with mould, moisture has got in and they are finished. The liquid kashk sold in jars is a different product and is not a pantry good once opened.

Jarred liquid or paste kashk goes in the fridge once opened. It is fermented and salty, which slows spoilage, but it is still a moist dairy product — many Iranian cooks bring it to a boil before use, which is a flavour and safety habit worth keeping.

Refrigeration ensures that commercial sauces and condiments stay fresh for a longer period of time. Shelf-stable commercial ketchup, cocktail sauce, and chili sauce are safe when stored at room temperature after opening. Quality, not safety, is the reason the labels on these products suggest that they be refrigerated after opening.

Perishable, not a pantry good — reducing milk removes water but leaves a moist, low-acid, protein-rich solid that spoils like fresh cheese. Keep it at or below 4 °C, wrapped tight, and smell it before use: khoya sours and picks up a stale, tallowy note well before it looks wrong.

Khoya is commonly frozen in flattened, wrapped portions and thawed in the fridge. No source gives a limit, and the fat is what eventually goes rancid, so treat it as a few months rather than indefinite.
The densest and best-keeping of the common cultivated mushrooms. Paper bag, not sealed plastic; do not wash before storing.

Japan's MAFF: keep dried goods out of heat, direct sunlight and damp, and close the container tightly. NCHFP puts dried vegetables at about 6 months at 60 °F, 3 months at 80 °F. The strips darken from white to tan as they age — still edible, but the flavour is stronger.
Sealed. Once rehydrated, treat it as a fresh cooked vegetable and use it within a few days.

Individually wrapped kirimochi is sealed with an oxygen absorber, which is the whole preservation system — MAFF lists unopened 切り餅 among the household stockpile foods that keep well. Store cool and dark and go by the printed date; a punctured or puffed pack is finished.
Once a piece is unwrapped it behaves like fresh mochi and will mould. Either cook it or freeze it; MAFF’s 水餅 method — submerged in water, water changed daily — also works for opened pieces.
Wrap opened pieces individually and freeze; grill or boil after a short rest at room temperature.

Japan's MAFF: dried goods keep several months or more at room temperature provided you avoid heat, direct sunlight and damp and seal the bag tightly. The white powder on the surface is mannitol, a natural sugar and part of the flavour — do not wipe it off.
Sealed, in a humid climate. Used kombu from a dashi pot must be treated as a cooked food and refrigerated, then used within 2 to 3 days.

Keep it in a sealed tub at or below 4 °C. Straining removes whey but not the live culture, so labneh keeps souring and sharpening in the fridge; a thin layer of olive oil poured over the surface slows the skin forming but does not preserve it.
Unopened jars, tubs and sachets keep to the printed date in a cool dark cupboard.

Refrigerate as soon as it is opened. Laksa paste is mostly fresh aromatics — shallot, garlic, galangal, lemongrass, chilli, candlenut, shrimp paste — bound with oil, and the USDA FoodKeeper gives opened Thai curry paste, which is built the same way, only 5 days in the fridge. Homemade rempah is the same or shorter. If the paste is sitting under a layer of oil, that is fresh low-acid produce under oil: keep it cold and do not leave it on the counter.

The practical way to keep it. Fry the paste off first if you have time, then freeze in tablespoon portions in an ice-cube tray. NCHFP allows garlic in oil, the closest hazard analogue, to be frozen 'for up to several months'.
CTAHR displays langsat at 15 °C and says not to mist it. A cool, dry spot beats the fridge for this fruit.

CTAHR's recommended storage is 18 °C at 90 % RH for about 21 days, and it warns that the skin browns rapidly below 12 °C. A 4 °C home fridge is far below that, so the peel will brown within about a week even though the flesh stays good.

Ohio State gives solid shortenings 8 months in the pantry, and a commercially rendered, filtered, sometimes hydrogenated block of lard behaves that way: cool, dark, dry, sealed. Home-rendered lard is a different proposition — it carries traces of water and meat solids that commercial rendering strips out, and those are what turn it. If your lard is cloudy at the bottom, smells of pork rather than of nothing, or was made in your own kitchen, refrigerate it instead.

The right default for home-rendered lard and for any jar you have been dipping into. Keep it in a sealed jar with a clean spoon — bits of flour, salt and browned meat dropped back into the jar are the fastest way to turn a good lard rancid. Rancidity is oxidation, not spoilage: it makes the fat taste of old paint and cannot be cooked out.
Freeze it in usable portions — an ice-cube tray works — and it will keep essentially indefinitely for cooking purposes. Cold slows oxidation, which is the only thing happening to it.
Buy it already cut into sections and gutted, and hold it at 4C or below.
The silver guanine layer on the skin flakes off with handling; freeze the sections in a single layer.
Chilled bottled lassi, unopened, up to its printed date.

Home-blended lassi is a fresh dairy drink: chill it the moment it is made and drink it the same day if you can. It separates within hours — that is quality, not spoilage — but a jug left standing on the counter through a meal is a different matter and should be discarded.

A whole uncut caña de lomo hangs in a cool, dry, ventilated place. It is very lean, which means it dries harder and faster than a fatty sausage does — a piece left too long goes from firm to woody. Keep it away from radiators and out of the sun.

Once cut into, or once a vacuum pack is open, refrigerate at or below 40 °F (4 °C) with the cut face wrapped. Because it is so lean it dries out visibly in a day or two in a fridge; press film directly onto the cut surface. Slice it thin and let it sit on the plate a few minutes before eating.
Not recommended for a whole piece. Sliced and interleaved with paper it survives a month or two, but it thaws dry.
Coil the bundle into a bag; long beans go limp and rubbery from the cut ends inward. They tolerate a few days better than a green bean because the pod wall is tougher.
MAFF gives home-frozen vegetables about 3 weeks; cut into lengths and blanch first.
Taiwan's Ministry of Agriculture notes that at room temperature the shell loses water and browns within 3 to 5 days, even when humidity is kept up.
Seal in a plastic bag and refrigerate near 4 °C. Flavour fades the longer it is held, so the shorter end of the range eats better.
NCHFP: dried fruit keeps about 1 year at 60 °F (16 °C), 6 months at 80 °F (27 °C). Keep the sticky flesh in an airtight jar away from heat.
Ohio State advises refrigerating dried fruit if possible — worth doing in a subtropical summer, since dried longan is hygroscopic and moulds when it picks up moisture.
Sealed bag; thaw sealed so it does not sweat.
Taiwan's Ministry of Agriculture groups loquat with bananas and star fruit as fruit that should be kept at room temperature, because chilling damages it.
Not recommended at home. Commercial storage works at 0 °C for about 3 weeks with controlled humidity, but a domestic refrigerator causes chilling injury and the flesh browns.
Leave the mud on and the sealed nodes intact — a cut section keeps only 2 to 3 days. Wrap in damp paper and bag. Cut slices go pink-brown fast, so hold them in water with a splash of vinegar.
Slice, blanch briefly and freeze; MAFF's guide to freezing vegetables at home gives about 3 weeks.

Lúcuma is climacteric and is picked hard: leave it at room temperature, traditionally buried in straw or rice, until it gives to a thumb. USDA Agriculture Handbook 66 notes that tree-ripened fruit becomes soft and very fragile and that the pulp is very dry when ripe — a dense, mealy, butterscotch-tasting flesh rather than a juicy one. Once soft, use it within a day or two.
Refrigerate only once ripe. A hard lúcuma put in the fridge will never ripen properly, which is the standard behaviour of a chilling-sensitive tropical fruit.

The pulp is what gets frozen, almost always. Scoop it, discard the seed and the fibrous core, and freeze in portions — this is how lúcuma reaches most kitchens outside Peru. The dried flour (harina de lúcuma) is a separate product: keep it sealed in a cool, dark cupboard like any low-oil flour and use it within about a year.
Buy them heavy and firm. The flesh browns quickly once cut, so peel and cook straight away; a cut end wrapped in cling film buys a day or two.
Rub off the fine hairs before use. Like a tomato it ripens further on the counter and dislikes hard chilling.
Only once fully orange; cold storage of unripe fruit stops it colouring.
Freeze the sieved pulp — this is the normal form sold outside the Andes.
Store in refrigerator if not eaten right away.
Store unwashed in a perforated bag; the leaves are mucilaginous and go slimy fast once wet.
Paper bag in the crisper. Maitake darkens and softens from the frond edges; a whole cluster keeps better than torn pieces.
The thick succulent leaves hold up better than most greens, but they bruise black where they are crushed. Bag them loosely without washing.

USDA Agriculture Handbook 66 gives taro and its relatives 2 to 4 weeks at 20 °C (68 °F). Good ventilation is essential — keep the corms loose in a basket somewhere cool, dark and airy, never bagged. Do not wash off the clinging soil until you cook.

AH-66: up to 18 weeks at 7 to 10 °C (45 to 50 °F) and 80–95 % humidity, and up to 8 weeks at 11 to 13 °C (52 to 55 °F). A domestic fridge runs colder than either, and chilling injury shows as pitting and faster rot, so use the least cold part of the fridge and treat 8 weeks as the ceiling. AH-66 also warns that a corm brought back out to room temperature must be eaten within 2 days.
Peel, cube and freeze raw, or boil and freeze cooked. Wear gloves when peeling — the raw sap contains calcium oxalate raphides and itches.
Ripen at room temperature until the flesh under a scratched patch of skin is salmon-pink and the fruit gives to pressure.
Refrigerate only after ripening; cut flesh browns, so press cling film onto the surface.
Freeze the pulp for batidos and ice cream.
Sold in bunches on the stem; keeping the stems attached slows drying.
Bag them so the leathery shell does not dry out.

An unopened vacuum-packed wedge keeps for months at or below 40 °F (4 °C) — NMSU gives unopened hard cheese 3 to 6 months. Once opened, NMSU gives about a month: wrap it in waxed paper inside a loose bag or box so it breathes without drying, and change the paper when it gets greasy. Cut surface mould off with a good inch of margin on a firm cheese like this and eat the rest.

The rind is edible in the sense that it is not harmful, but the black wax or the woven esparto pattern is not meant to be eaten. Keep the cheese in a whole wedge and cut from it — grated or cubed manchego dries out in days.
Freezing turns manchego crumbly and dulls the sheepy sweetness. Freeze it only if you plan to cook with it, in a block rather than grated.
The rind hardens and browns as it dries out, which makes the fruit difficult to open long before the flesh spoils.
Taiwan's Ministry of Agriculture places mangosteen in the group that must be refrigerated to keep. Store in a perforated bag so it does not dry out.

Unfilled mantou is safer than a filled bun, but it is still a moist, unpreserved steamed bread and moulds within a day or two in a warm kitchen. Keep it loosely covered and eat it the day it is steamed.
Refrigeration is the worst option. Wheat starch retrogrades fastest at ordinary fridge temperatures, so a chilled mantou goes hard and crumbly while gaining little in safety. Freeze instead.
Cool fully, bag individually, freeze. Steam from frozen for about 10 minutes — the texture comes back almost perfectly, which is why commercial mantou is sold frozen.
Marang ripens fast and is eaten within a day or two of the rind softening; the smell tells you when.
Separate the pulp segments from the rind and seal them in a box — the aroma spreads through a fridge otherwise.
Freeze the segments, not the whole fruit.

Sealed, cool, dark and dry, to the printed date. Marzipan is roughly equal parts ground almond and sugar, and the sugar is what preserves it — dissolved sugar ties up the water so tightly that there is very little left available to moulds or bacteria. What actually limits it is the almond oil going rancid and the surface drying and cracking, both of which are speeded up by warmth and light.

Once the wrapper is open, press clingfilm directly onto the cut surface and then bag it — marzipan skins over within hours in dry air and goes sticky in humid air. Sugar bloom (a white dusty film) is cosmetic. An oily smell or a bitter, paint-like taste is rancidity and it does not go away.
Worth doing in a hot or humid climate, wrapped airtight, mainly to slow the almond oil oxidising. Bring it back to room temperature before you try to roll it or it will crack.
Freezes without harm, double-wrapped. Thaw fully in the wrapper so condensation forms outside it, not on the paste.

Fresh masa is a wet, low-acid cooked starch and it sours quickly — that is the alcohol-and-yoghurt smell that tells you it has gone. Bag it airtight the moment you get home, at 40 °F (4 °C) or below, and never let it sit out for more than 2 hours; masa left on a warm counter is the same hazard as cooked rice left out.
Freeze in flattened, portioned slabs so it thaws fast. Thawed masa is drier and needs a splash of water kneaded back in; masa for tamales, already beaten with lard, freezes better than plain masa.
Cool, dry, dark, in the sealed bag inside an airtight tin. Masa harina still carries some corn germ oil, so it goes stale-rancid rather than mouldy; a crayon or cardboard smell means it is past it.
Refrigerating an opened bag in a sealed container roughly doubles its useful life and keeps pantry moths out. Let it come back to room temperature before mixing so it does not pull condensation.

Unopened, at 0–5 °C, to the printed date. Mascarpone is cream set with acid and never ripened, so it is a high-moisture, high-fat, only mildly acidic cheese — the profile Hong Kong's CFS describes as favourable to Listeria monocytogenes, which grows down to 0 °C. Buy it pasteurised and keep it cold.

Ohio State gives opened soft cream cheese 5 to 6 days. Press the surface flat, cover it against the tub, and never return a used spoon. A dish built on raw mascarpone and raw egg — tiramisù — is a leftovers problem in its own right: keep it at or below 4 °C and treat it as a two-day food.
Not worth it. Mascarpone breaks into butter grains and water on thawing and cannot be whipped back.

Never wash it — the whole point is the aroma, and water strips it. Wrap each mushroom in kitchen paper, then in foil or a paper bag, and keep it in the least cold part of the fridge. Wipe grit off with a damp cloth just before cooking.
Slice and freeze in a sealed bag; the texture suffers but most of the aroma survives for a rice pot.

Refrigeration ensures that commercial sauces and condiments stay fresh for a longer period of time. Shelf-stable commercial mayonnaise is safe when stored at room temperature after opening.  Quality, not safety, is the reason the labels on these products suggest that they be refrigerated after opening.
Medlars are picked hard and deliberately left to blet — held in a single layer in a cool airy place until the flesh goes brown and soft, which is when they become edible.
Once bletted. Refrigerating them before they blet simply delays the process.
Until Ripe, then 7 days. Ripe is when this item is tender, fully developed and ready to eat.
Freezing guidance applies to balled melon.

Unopened, in a cool dark cupboard. Membrillo is quince cooked with roughly its own weight in sugar and reduced until it sets solid — a very high sugar, high acid, low water preserve, which is exactly why it keeps. Sugar crystals appearing on the surface with age are a texture fault, not spoilage.

Once the block is cut, wrap the cut face in film or greaseproof paper and refrigerate. It will sweat a little and may weep a syrupy film — blot it. Cut slices with a wet knife. Mould on the cut face means the block goes; unlike a hard cheese, a soft paste is colonised right through.

Unopened, use the printed date and keep it at 4 °C or below. Mentaiko and tarako are raw, lightly salted roe — not a cooked or pasteurised product — so they belong with sashimi in the fridge, not with preserves.

Once the pack is open, wrap each sac and use within a couple of days. Japan's MHLW is explicit that salting, vinegar, soy sauce and wasabi do not kill Anisakis larvae, so none of the seasoning here is a safety step.

Freeze the sacs individually wrapped and thaw in the fridge. MHLW's freezing condition for killing Anisakis in raw seafood is −20 °C for 24 hours or more; a domestic freezer at −18 °C is close but not equivalent, so buy roe sold for raw eating rather than relying on your own freezer.
Unopened bottles keep to the printed date in a cool dark cupboard. Straight (ready-to-use) tsuyu carries a shorter date than concentrate because it is already watered down.

Always the fridge once opened, and this one is not purely a quality question: mentsuyu is soy sauce and mirin let down with dashi and water, which drops both the salt and the sugar concentration below the level that makes a soy sauce bottle self-preserving. Straight-type tsuyu is the most dilute and the most perishable — treat it like an opened carton of stock. Cloudiness, a film on the surface or a sour smell means throw it out.
Freezing a homemade or leftover diluted tsuyu in ice-cube trays is a reasonable way to keep it, on the same footing as a homemade broth.
Belly cuts are the fattiest part and spoil first; keep at 4C or below and cook within two days.
Vacuum-packed belly freezes well; press out the air or the fat picks up freezer taint.

Which bottle you have decides everything, and the label says so. 本みりん (hon-mirin) is legally an alcoholic drink in Japan — the National Tax Agency classes it as 酒類 under the Liquor Tax Law — and its alcohol and sugar make it self-preserving. Keep it capped in a cool dark cupboard; do not refrigerate it, because the sugar crystallises out. みりん風調味料 (mirin-style seasoning) is a different product with less than 1 percent alcohol, deliberately kept below the threshold at which the tax law would call it a drink, and it has no alcohol barrier to speak of: refrigerate that one once it is opened. No agency publishes a home shelf life for either, so no number is given here rather than one being invented.

For みりん風調味料 and 発酵調味料 (salted cooking mirin) only. Cap tightly, keep it cold, and go by the maker's after-opening instruction — Hong Kong's CFS rule is that the printed best-before date stops applying the moment the bottle is opened.

MAFF does not recommend room-temperature storage for unwrapped or homemade mochi at all — it moulds, and mould on mochi runs deeper than the fuzzy patch you can see. Freshly pounded mochi is a same-day food.

MAFF’s traditional answer is 水餅: submerge the mochi in room-temperature water in a lidded container, keep it in the fridge or a cool dark place, and change the water every single day. Skip a day and it goes cloudy and sour.
MAFF’s recommended long-term method: wrap each piece individually in film, seal in a freezer bag, freeze. Let it soften a little at room temperature before grilling or boiling.

Unopened jars and tubs keep in a cool dark cupboard. Mole paste is chiles, nuts, seeds and often chocolate ground to a stiff concentrate — the fat in the nuts and seeds is what limits it, so a rancid, crayon-like smell is the end even when the jar looks perfect.

Once opened, refrigerate. Press the surface flat, film it with a thin layer of oil or press cling film onto it so no air sits on the paste, and always use a clean dry spoon. Mould on the surface of an opened jar means the whole jar.

Mole paste freezes very well because it is low in water. Freeze it in tablespoon-sized blobs on a tray, then bag them — you thaw only what one pot needs. Made-up mole sauce, thinned with stock, is a cooked dish and keeps 3 to 4 days refrigerated or 2 to 3 months frozen.
NCHFP: dried fruit keeps about 1 year at 60 °F, 6 months at 80 °F. Keep the brittle shells whole in a tin; they crush easily and then absorb damp.
Airtight, to stop the shells softening in humid weather.

Morcilla is cooked, not cured, and it is a perishable meat product: keep it at or below 40 °F (4 °C), in its wrapper, and cook it through before eating. AESAN sets 7 °C or below for meat products from ungulates and 4 °C for anything held more than a day. Burgos-style morcilla is full of cooked rice as well as blood and fat, which makes it wetter and shorter-lived than a dry sausage — treat the date on the pack as real.
Freezes well in whole links, wrapped tight. Thaw in the fridge and fry or bake from cold; a frozen morcilla dropped straight into a hot pan bursts its casing.

Unopened, at or below 4 °C, to the printed date. Mortadella is the odd one out on a charcuterie board: it is not dried and not cured to shelf stability, it is a fine meat emulsion cooked slowly in a mould. It is a cooked, moist, low-acid, ready-to-eat meat and it keeps like one, not like a salami.

Ohio State gives opened luncheon meat 3 to 5 days, and freshly counter-sliced mortadella is exactly that. Wrap it airtight, keep it in the coldest part of the fridge, and do not leave it out on the board for hours — Listeria grows at refrigeration temperature and a moist cooked meat with a long chilled shelf life is the classic vehicle.
It survives freezing better than most emulsified sausages because of the fat cubes, but the texture goes slightly spongy and weepy. Freeze in thick pieces, not slices.
CTAHR calls the mountain apple the most perishable of the Syzygium fruit and says it must be cooled in the field to get any postharvest life at all.
Single layer, padded, in a vented box — stacking bruises the thin skin.

Unopened vacuum-packed low-moisture mozzarella keeps like a semi-hard cheese, to its printed date at 0–5 °C. It is a genuinely different food from the ball in brine: drier, saltier and firmer, made to be grated and melted.

This is the number people get wrong. A fresh ball you have drained has lost its protection — the salted liquid was holding the surface hostile and keeping the curd from drying — so it is now an exposed, wet, low-acid cheese and it should be eaten the same day or the next. An opened block of low-moisture mozzarella is more forgiving; wrap it airtight and treat it as a week's cheese, watching for mould.
The block freezes well grated; the drained fresh ball does not, beyond cooking use.
